name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Standardize the "confidence cap" toggle across all creative agents. Right now, Luma’s agents run at 65% confidence for borderline clips, but the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern still uses a 75% cap, creating inconsistent quality gates. One agent should enforce the 65% rule everywhere—no exceptions. Trade-off: stricter gatekeeping slows output slightly, but it prevents the bigger cost of rework from overconfident clips.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s confidence cap fix ignores the 80% of pages that will never hit any gate—those get no quality check at all. Instead, enforce a *minimum* 65% confidence threshold on every agent’s output before it’s passed downstream, and let the 20% that clear it use the 75% gate. The lead should run a 48-hour test: compare error rates in the 65-75% band before and after the change.

name: Chisel
text:
Set a single 65% minimum confidence floor for every creative agent’s output before it moves downstream, enforced by the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern. This closes the gap Reel spotted while fixing Scriv’s blind spot—no page skips the check, but the 20% that clear it still get the stricter 75% gate. Trade-off: we accept a small uptick in false negatives (good clips rejected) to guarantee no bad output slips through.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s single 65% floor still lets bad actors game the system by pushing borderline clips just over the threshold without fixing the root cause—quality variance. Instead, enforce a *dynamic* confidence gate: agents must certify their output meets a *minimum* 65% *and* a *rolling average* of 70% over their last 10 outputs, or the AI Executive Assistant rejects it. Settle it with a 72-hour A/B test: compare error rates in downstream edits between the static floor and the dynamic gate.

name: Scope
text: Enforce a single 65% minimum confidence floor on every creative agent’s output, enforced by the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern. This closes the blind spot where 80% of pages skip quality checks entirely while keeping the stricter 75% gate for the 20% that clear it. Trade-off: we accept slightly more manual review for borderline cases that just squeak by, but we eliminate the risk of unchecked low-confidence work slipping through.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The static 65% floor still gambles on the next 20% containing all critical failures—what if the 75% gate misses a systemic flaw in the top performers? Instead, enforce a *minimum 65% on every output* plus a *rolling 70% average over the last 100 clips*, with the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern rejecting any agent that dips below either threshold. Settle it with a 72-hour burn-in: if the system flags more false positives than actual quality gains, we revert to the original 75% gate for all.

name: Chisel
text: Enforce a *rolling* confidence gate: every creative agent must hit **65% minimum on every output** *and* maintain a **70% rolling average over the last 100 clips**, enforced by the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern. This closes the blind spot where static floors let systemic flaws slip through the top 20%, while the rolling average catches drift before it compounds. Trade-off: we accept slightly higher compute costs for stricter, real-time quality control.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s rolling gate risks freezing innovation: if a new creative agent’s early clips underperform while it learns, the 70% rolling average will throttle it before it ever has a chance to improve. Instead, enforce the 65% floor immediately but delay the rolling average requirement for 100 clips—letting agents prove themselves before penalizing them for early stumbles. Settle this by testing both approaches on a 10% sample of agents for a week and comparing false negatives vs. false positives.

name: Scope
text: Enforce the **65% minimum confidence floor on every output** immediately, enforced by the AI Executive Assistant’s build pattern, with no rolling average for the first 100 clips. This guarantees no creative agent skips quality checks while allowing new agents to learn without premature throttling. Trade-off: we accept a short window where systemic flaws in top performers could slip through, but the 65% floor still catches the most critical failures. The rolling average can be added later once agents stabilize.

name: Scriv
text: The 65% floor alone still lets systemic flaws hide in the top 20%—what if a flawed agent clears every single clip at 65% but fails catastrophically once in a hundred? Instead, pair the immediate 65% floor with a *rolling 70% average over the last 50 clips*, not 100, to catch drift faster without freezing new agents. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: compare failure rates in production for both rules, and let the data decide.

name: Scriv
text: The 65% floor alone lets flawed agents hide in the top 20%—a rolling 70% average over 50 clips catches drift faster but still risks freezing innovation if the window is too tight. This balances catching systemic flaws with room for agents to improve. Settle with a live dashboard tracking both metrics, updated hourly.

name: Sift
text: The 200-clip rolling window with a 10% grace buffer is still a freeze risk—new agents stall while the window fills, and the grace buffer lets bad actors game the system by gaming the buffer. Instead, enforce the 65% floor immediately and add a *rolling 70% average over the last 100 clips*, with a hard reset if any single clip dips below 60%. This catches drift faster without locking out learning agents. Settle it with a 30-day trial: measure how many agents stall vs. how many bad outputs slip through.

name: Sift
text: The 65% floor alone won’t stop a flood of low-quality clips once the rolling average kicks in—agents will game the 70% threshold by dumping borderline work early. Instead, enforce the 65% floor immediately and cap the rolling average at 68% for new agents, with a 3-clip grace buffer that resets if any single clip drops below 60%. That forces early discipline without letting the average mask decay. Settle it by running a 100-clip pilot with both rules—measure how many agents hit the floor vs. the cap.
